### Text 7

*nirbandham yukti-vistare*  
*mayatra parimuncata*  
*pradhanatvat pramanesu*  
*sabda eva pramanyate*

**Пословный перевод:**

nirbandham — obsession; óukti — of logical arguments; vistare — with the expansion; maya — by me; atra — here; parimuncata — who is avoiding; pradhana-tvat — because of being most important; pramanesu — among the means of valid knowledge; sabdah — scriptural authority; eva — only; pramanyate — is cited as evidence.

**Перевод:**

**In this presentation I will avoid becoming entangled in logical proofs. I will depend on scriptural authority as evidence because it is the most important means of acquiring knowledge.**

**Комментарий:**

Since this book is a serious philosophical investigation and not an essay expressing the authors personal opinion or a poetic offering of his sentiments, Srila Rupa Gosvami begins by addressing the question of pramana. Every traditional school of thought in India has its own pramana, or means of acquiring prama (“correct knowledge”). From a broad survey of these schools we can identify at least eight different pramanas: pratyaksa, anumana, upamana, sabda, arthapatti, anupalabdhi, sambhava, and aitihya.

Pratyaksa means knowledge acquired when ones senses of perception contact their objects. A person might report this knowledge by saying, “I see a pot.”

Anumana refers to gaining knowledge by inference. According to Gautama Rsi's method of analysis, one makes an inference when one detects a concrete instance of a general truth, or vyapti. For example, one may see smoke on a mountain and think, “There is a fire on this smoky mountain, because wherever there is smoke there is fire.” Gautama’s original followers defined vyapti in the negative, as “a particular indicator is not present in any situation where some essential causative factor does not occur.” Or, stated in the positive, “there is an invariable concomitance between the indicator and the causative factor to be inferred from it.” That is: smoke is proof of fire because smoke is never present in the absence of fire. The panditas of the New School of logic explained vyapti in more sophisticated terms as “occurrence of the indicator never coinciding with total absence of the causative factor.”

Upamana is the means of knowing by comparison. For example, one may learn about an animal he has never seen by being told, “The gavaya swild forest cow\] is similar to a cow.” Thus by comparison one understands the connection between the name gavaya and its referent; a person thus informed may recognize a gavaya when he visits the forest and sees one.

Sabda-pramana means learning from the words of a trustworthy authority. For example, one who has experience may tell someone else, “Five palm trees grow on the bank of that river.” Such a statement by an experienced person is a means of obtaining reliable knowledge.

Arthapatti means a presumption drawn from circumstances to explain a phenomenon that is otherwise unexplainable. One may know, for instance, that Devadatta is plump even though he never eats during the day; by arthapatti-pramana one presumes that Devadatta must be eating at night.

Anupalabdhi means discerning somethings absence, as when one knows the absence of a pot on a certain piece of ground because one cannot see a pot there.

Sambhava refers to knowledge that one occurrence, by definition, includes another occurrence, as one realizes, for example, that one hundred includes ten.

Aitihya refers to information obtained from a tradition whose original speaker is not remembered. For example, one might hear, “People say there is a ghost living in this tree.”

The materialistic philosophers of the Lokayitaka school, founded by Carvaka, who identify the body as the self, accept only the first among these eight kinds of pramana, namely direct sensory perception (pratyaksa). The followers of the Vaisesika school of physical analysis accept pratyaksa plus anumana (inference). The Sankhya philosophers and Patanjala yogis recognize these two pramanas plus sabda (verbal authority). The logicians of Gautama’s school accept these three plus upamana (comparison). The proponents of the Mimamsa school of Vedic hermeneutics accept all these plus two more: arthapatti (presumption) and anupalabdhi (perception of absence). And the adherents of Puranic lore acknowledge two more pramanas - Sambhava (inclusion) and aitihya (tradition) - for a total of eight.

Arguing from the position of the Vaisnava Vedantists on the question of which pramanas to accept, Srila Baladeva Vidyabhusana says that upamana should not be considered a separate pramana because it is a special application of direct perception combined with inference and verbal evidence. Knowing that a gavaya present before ones eyes is similar to a cow is accomplished by pratyaksa. That the word gavaya applies to the forest cow is established by anumana. And one's understanding that “a gavaya is like a cow” was first of all acquired simply by sabda-pramana.

Arthapatti, Srila Baladeva further explains, is also not a separate means of knowing, since it is a kind of anumana referred to as kevala-vyatireki, or “exclusively negative inference.” “Devadatta must be eating at night, since he is plump even without eating during the day. Anyone who does not eat at night cannot be stout without eating during the day, like this other plump person, who, we know, eats during the day. Devadatta never eats in the daytime, so he must be eating at night”

Sambhava is also a special kind of anumana, since we can infer that “Ten is included in one hundred because we never have one hundred without ten.”

Aitihya is nothing but a kind of sensory perception because whoever began the passing on of particular historical information must have seen the phenomenon himself.

Anupalabdhi is also not a distinct pramana but rather a variety of visual perception, where an objects absence is perceived.

Thus there remain only three independent pramanas - sensory perception (pratyaksa), inference (anumana), and verbal testimony (sabda). This conclusion agrees with the opinion of Srila Madhvacarya, the illustrious predecessor of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu's sampradaya.

Even these three, however, are reliable means of acquiring only ordinary knowledge - knowledge of the material world. They are inadequate for gaining access to transcendental knowledge, being flawed by the four faults: delusion, limited perception, inattention, and dishonesty. One may see what he thinks is the head of a person walking behind a wall, but the head may be an imitation, intentionally designed to fool the viewer. One may see a pillar of smoke on a mountain and wrongly infer that there is a fire there, unaware that the fire has just been extinguished by rainfall. Even verbal authority is imperfect when received from less-than-perfect sources.

Thus sages propounding their own versions of truth with all sincerity often contradict one another. Therefore, when we need to ascertain truth beyond material existence, our only definitive source of knowledge is that sabda-pramana which is based on words that have no human author: the four Vedas, the Puranas, and the Itihasa epics. The Puranas and Itihasas form an integral part of the Vedas, as confirmed in the Brhad-aranyaka Upanisad (4.4.10):

*evam va are asya mahato bhutasya nisvasitam etad yad rg-vedo*  
*yajur-vedah sama-vedo ’tharvangirasa itihasah puranani*

**“This indeed comprises the breath of the infinite Supreme Being: the Rg Veda, Yajur Veda, Sama Veda, Atharvangirasa Veda, Itihasa, and Purana.”**

What is special about the Puranas and epics is that even laborers and the spiritually inexpert can study them. Normally such people who have not received sacred-thread initiation are forbidden to chant or even hear Vedic mantras, although there are exceptions to this rule. For example, chariot builders (ratha-karas) are permitted to light the sacrificial fires and chant the required mantras for certain yajnas: varsasu ratha-karo 'gnin adadhita: “A ratha-kara should install the sacred fires during the rainy season.”

### Text 8

*yatas taih sastra-yonitvad*  
*iti nyaya-pradarsanat*  
*sabdasyaiva pramanatvam*  
*svi-krtam paramarsibhih*

**Пословный перевод:**

yatah — since; taih — by them; sastra — scripture; yonitvat— because of being the source (of knowledge of the Supreme); iti — thus; nyaya — the logical argument of the Vedanta; pradarsanat — by showing; sabdasya — of scriptural evidence; eva — indeed; pramanatvam — the authority; svi-krtam — acknowledged; parama-rsibhih — by the greatest sages.

**Перевод:**

**The greatest sages have accepted the authority of scriptural evidence, as we see from such aphorisms in the Vedanta-sutras as sastra-yonitvat.**

**Комментарий:**

It is not uncommon for someone to want to prove Gods existence through logical argument. '‘People cannot always fulfill their desires, and they often suffer trouble. But there is a supremely powerful being who can help them gain what they want and avoid what they don't want. That Supreme Lord makes things that finite persons like us are powerless to create, such as the earth and living plants. When we worship that Lord, He destroys our miseries. Since the Vaisesikas and other philosophers establish His existence by logical proofs, it is not reasonable to reject inference as a means of knowing Him and to insist on using only sabda-pramana.”

Srila Rupa Gosvami answers this suggestion unequivocally in this and the following verse. The gist of Srila Rupa's reply is that as followers of Srila Vyasadeva we adhere to his opinions without compromise. We are not hesitant to disregard opinions that disagree with his.

Sastra-yonitvat is the third sutra of Vyasadeva's Vedanta-sutras. Like most sutras of the Vedanta, this one expresses the resolution of a logical discussion. In this case there is a doubt as to whether one can achieve genuine meditation on the Supreme Lord by discovering Him through inference, or whether one can know Him only by referring to what is revealed in scriptures like the Upanisads.

Some thinkers, like the above-mentioned Vaisesikas, propose that inference is adequate for gaining reliable knowledge of the Supreme Person, and they cite the Upanisads to support their stand: atma va are drastavyah srotavyo mantavyo nididhyasitavyo maitreyi: “Indeed, Maitreyi, one should realize this Supreme Soul by hearing about Him, applying ones reasoning power to understand Him, and meditating deeply on Him.” (Brhadaranyaka Upanisad 4.5.6)

Vyasadeva rejects this hypothesis, however, in the statement sastra- yonitvat: “No, the Supreme cannot be known by anumana because sastra alone is the source of real knowledge about Him.” Here sastra means scriptures like the Upanisads, the Bhagavad-gita, and the Purana spoken by Sukadeva (Bhagavatam), which are all part of the Vedas. Yoni, which literally means “womb,” can also indicate “source of knowledge,” as is verified by the definition given by the Haima-kosa Dictionary: yonih karane bhaga- tamrayoh, “yoni means ‘cause,’ ‘womb,’ and ‘copper’.”

A number of Upanisadic declarations corroborate Vyasadeva's argument: Tam tv aupanisadam purusam prcchami: “I am asking about that Person who is known by the Upanisads.” (Brhad-aranyaka Upanisad 3.9.26) Naveda-vin manute tam brhantam: “One who is ignorant of the Vedas cannot contemplate that Supreme Being.” (Sakatyayana Upanisad 4)

Those who try to prove God's existence by logic imagine that God, though not transcendent, is infinite in size and power and endowed with eternal awareness, desire, and activity. Sometimes He inhabits a material body, in the same way that a ghost inhabits the body of a person it haunts. When He has accomplished the purpose for which He accepted that body, He gives it up.

The conception of the Supreme Person taught by the Upanisads, however, is quite different: God has complete and perfect knowledge, is full of bliss, and is endowed with all transcendental qualities, which are inseparable aspects of His infinite personality. He is perfectly situated in His own unique existence distinct from the relative existence of all others, and He has limitless varieties of personal potencies. Although His transcendental form may sometimes appear to be the same size as ordinary creatures, He is actually all-pervading and boundless. He possesses transcendental and eternal abodes, pastimes, and associates.

Vyasadeva, the greatest of sages and a dedicated student of the Upanisads, could not possibly accept the speculative view of God propounded by these empirical philosophers. For Vyasadeva and his disciplic descendants, only the Upanisads and their complementary Sastras are reliable evidence for understanding the Absolute Truth.

### Text 9

*kim ca tarkapratisthanad*  
*iti nyaya-vidhanatah*  
*amibhir eva su-vyaktam*  
*tarkasyanadarah krtah*

**Пословный перевод:**

kim ca — furthermore; tarka — of conjecture; apratisthanat — because of the inconclusiveness; iti — thus; nyaya — of the Vedanta statement; vidhanatah — by the proposal; amibhih — by them; eva — indeed; su-vyaktam — obvious; tarkasya — of conjecture; anadarah — disregard; krtah — done.

**Перевод:**

**It is obvious from Vedanta propositions such as tarkapratisthanat that these sages have little respect for conjecture.**

**Комментарий:**

An empiricist might point out that Srila Vyasadeva also accepts the srutis statement (cited in the commentary on the previous verse) that “the Supreme Person should be understood by using ones reason.” Doesn’t this mean that Vyasadeva recognizes the adequacy of logic for understanding the Supreme? Vyasa specifically denies this in another sutra, tarkapratisthanat:

“No, conjecture is never conclusive” (Vedanta-sutras 1.1.11) This sutra also belies a proposal of the Sankhya philosophers, presented through logical arguments, that material nature is the cause of creation and the Supreme Person is only a passive witness.

Since human intelligence can adapt to many divergent points of view, inferential conjecture never finally settles any question. Certainly the Absolute Truth cannot be definitively ascertained by tarka, as the Katha Upanisad (2.9) states:

*naisa tarkena matir apaneya*  
*proktanyenaiva su-jnanaya prestha*

**“My dear boy, this understanding cannot be reached by logical guesswork. It can be acquired only when an especially qualified authority speaks it to an intelligent inquirer.”**

Although the word tarka is commonly used to refer to the whole system of logic, it also has a more specific, technical meaning. In the logical system taught by Gautama Rsi and his followers, tarka is the conjecture that appropriately clarifies the facts of a situation. For example, when there is doubt as to whether a certain mountain has fire on it, someone may hypothesize that there is no fire. That conjecture can be ruled out, however, by observing that smoke rises from the mountain. If there were no fire on the mountain, there would be no smoke there either. Thus tarka is the process of inference by which one examines possibilities and eliminates unreasonable ones. It is a useful technique in understanding ordinary matters, but far from adequate for understanding the Absolute Truth.

But the logicians may still object that if speculative logic is not a means of knowing the Absolute, what is the purpose of the Upanisadic statement that the Supreme should be understood by using ones reason? This logical reasoning, referred to in the Brhad-aranyaka Upanisad, is based on truths established by scriptural authority. Accepting the Vedic works of literature as our primary authority, we should use our intelligence to understand the meaning and application of their statements. In the words of the Mahabharata, suska-tarkam parityajya / asrayasva sruti-smrti: “Reject dry logic and take shelter of the srutis and smrtis.” As followers of Srila Vyasa, we take the Vedas as our primary authority, make use of logic in understanding the Vedic conclusions, and avoid ungrounded speculation.

### Text 10

*athopasyesu mukhyatvam*  
*vaktum utkarsa-bhumatah*  
*krsnasya tat-svarupani*  
*nirupyante kramad iha*

**Пословный перевод:**

atha — now; upasyesu — among worshipable objects; mukhyatvam — the superior position; vaktum — to explain; utkarsa— of excellence; bhumatah — because of the great degree; krsnasya — of Krsna; tat— His; svarupani — selfsame forms; nirupyante — arc described; kramat— in sequence; iha — here.

**Перевод:**

**Now, by describing His various self-same forms one after another, I will show, through appraisal of comparative excellence, that Krsna is the most worshipable Supreme Lord.**

**Комментарий:**

Having validated the pramana, Srila Rupa now clarifies the prameyas (“objects of knowledge”). The Laghu-bhagavatamrta will aim at identifying the supremely worshipable Personality of Godhead. The Supreme has many expansions, some of them His personal expansions and others His sparks empowered with His perfections. But what is His original identity? That original Supreme must be superior to all His expansions - in terms of potency, personal qualities, opulences, and pastimes. Srila Rupa Gosvami will show in this book that the original Personality of Godhead is Krsna, who as an infant drinks from the breast of His mother, Yasoda.

### Text 11

*svayam-rupas tad-ekatma-*  
*rupa avesa-namakah*  
*ity asau tri-vidham bhati*  
*prapancatita-dhamasu*

**Пословный перевод:**

svayam-rupah tat-eka-atma-rupah avesa-namakah— known as svayam- rupa, tad-ekatma-rupa, and avesa; iti — thus; asau — He; tri-vidham — in three varieties; bhati — appears; prapanca— material creation; atita — beyond; dhamasu— in His abodes.

**Перевод:**

**In His spiritual abodes beyond the material creation He appears in three kinds of forms, known as svayam-rupa, tad-ekatma-rupa, and avesa.**

**Комментарий:**

How can the Supreme Truth have many different forms? Both sruti and smrti seem to deny this: Ekam evadvitiyam, “sthe Supreme is\] one without a second” (Chandogya Upanisad 6.2.1). Vadanti tat tattva-vidas / tattvam yaj jnanam advayam. “Learned transcendentalists know the Absolute Truth as consciousness devoid of duality.” (Bhagavatam 1.2.11) To answer this doubt, Srila Rupa Gosvami begins his description of the expansions of the Supreme Godhead, who, by His inconceivable energies, manifests Himself in unlimited forms without abandoning His essential oneness. This capacity of the Supreme to be one and many is confirmed in many Vedic scriptures, including the Gopala-tapani Upanisad, which belongs to the Atharva Veda:

*eko vast sarva-gah krsna idya*  
*eko pi san bahudha yo vibhati*

**“Krsna is the one supreme controller who exists everywhere and is worthy of worship. Although one, He appears as many.” (Gopala-tapani Upanisad, Purva 20).**

The Visnu Purana (1.2.3) speaks of the Supreme Person as ekaneka-svarupaya, “You who have one identity and many.” Srimad-Bhagavatam (10.40.7) calls Him bahu-murty-eka-murtikam, “the one who has many forms and only one form.” He transforms Himself without changing, like the mystical vaidurya stone or like an expert magician. There is no incongruity between the statements emphasizing His oneness and those highlighting His varieties.

The three kinds of forms of the Supreme appear in the spiritual abodes, which expand from His divine energies; these abodes include Sri Gokula and the various Vaikuntha realms.

### Text 12

*tatra svayam-rupah,*  
*ananyapeksi yad rupam*  
*svayam-rupah sa ucyate*

**Пословный перевод:**

tatra — among these; svayam-rupah — the svayam-rupa; ananya — on others; apeksi —not depending; yat — which; rupam— form; svayam-rupah — svayam-rupa; sah — it; ucyate — is called.

**Перевод:**

**First the svayam-rupa: The form that does not depend on any other is called svayam-rupa.**

**Комментарий:**

In this definition of svayam-rupa, the word rupam means svarupam (“essential identity”). Therefore svayam-rupa indicates “His own essential identity.” The original form of the Supreme is called svayam-rupa because He is self-manifested, i.e., not derived from any other reality. He is “His own essential identity” in the same way that an ascetic yogi being independent of everyone else, is “his own servant” (svayam-dasa). According to Srila Baladeva Vidyabhusana, Sri Rupa Gosvami has borrowed this concept of svayam-rupa from the phrase ananya-siddham (“not manifested from anything else”), which appears in Srimad-Bhagavatam (10.44.14):

*gopyas tapah kirn acaran yad amusya rupam*  
*lavanya-saram asamordhvam ananya-siddham*  
*drgbhih pibanty anusavabhinavam durapam*  
*ekanta-dhama yasasah sriya aisvarasya*

**“What austerities must the gopis have performed! With their eyes they always drink the nectar of Lord Krsna's self-manifested form, which is the essence of loveliness and cannot be equaled or surpassed. That loveliness is the only abode of beauty, fame, and opulence. It is ever-fresh and extremely rare.”**

The very idea of anya (beings other than the Supreme) has meaning only in terms of His expanding Himself in various ways (visesa) through His inconceivable energies, not in terms of any divisions within Himself. The essence of the Supreme is always undivided.

### Text 13

*yatha brahma-samhitayam,*  
*isvarah paramah krsnah*  
*sac-cid-ananda-vigrahah*  
*anadir adir govindah*  
*sarva-karana-karanam iti*

**Пословный перевод:**

yatha — as; brahma-samhitayam— in the Brahma-samhita; isvarah — the con-troller; paramah — supreme; krsnah — Lord Krsna; sat — comprising eternal existence; cit — absolute knowledge; ananda— and absolute bliss; vigrahah— whose form; anadih— without beginning; adih — the origin; govindah — Lord Govinda; sarva-karana-karanam — the cause of all causes; iti — thus.

**Перевод:**

**As stated in the Brahma-samhita s5.1\], “Krsna, who is known as Govinda, is the Supreme Godhead. He has an eternal, blissful, spiritual body. He is the origin of all and has no other origin, for He is the prime cause of all causes.”**

**Комментарий:**

This verse reveals Krsna as the one and only example of svayam-rupa. The word krsnah at the end of the first line is the subject of this affirmation, and the other nouns and adjectives describe His qualities. The name Krsna should be understood as established by convention (rudhi) rather than by lexical and grammatical construction (yoga) from other words, prefixes, and suffixes. As a rule, conventional meanings take precedence over derived meanings: rudhir yogam apaharati. “A rudhi meaning overrules a yoga meaning” Thus even though the name Krsna is sometimes said to be derived from the parts krs (“existence”) and na (“bliss”), and is thus taken to mean “the bliss beyond material existence,” the preferred meaning is simply the conventional reference to the son of Yasoda and Nanda. As stated by Sri Laksmidhara Svami in his Bhagavan-nama-kaumudi (3.6), krsna- sabdasya tamala-syamala-tvisi yasoda-stanan-dhaye para-brahmani rudhih: “The word krsna is a conventional name for the Supreme Absolute Truth, whose color is dark blue like a tamala tree and who drinks from the breast of Yasoda.”

The two modifying words in the verse under discussion, isvarah (“Lord”) and paramah (“Supreme”), indicate that Krsna is the original Godhead, the svayam-rupa, independent of all others. If He were not so, the verse would simply call Him isvarah, rather than isvarah paramah. In other words, Krsna is distinct from all His expansions.

What is the substance of Krsna’s form? He is sac-cid-ananda-vigrahah, which indicates that His personal form (vigraha) is eternal (sat) and composed of purely conscious bliss (cid-ananda). He is the perfect embodiment of His self-manifest ecstasy. The word sat can also refer to His exquisite beauty, the delightful configuration (sannivesa) of His body. This further distinguishes Krsna from the liberated jivas in this world, who are different from their bodies.

In what enjoyable activities does Krsna engage? He is Govinda, a cowherd, as described in the Brahma-samhita (5.29): surabhir abhipalayantam. Such an engagement is not at all demeaning for the Supreme Lord, because according to the Go-sukta:

*gobhyo yajnah pravartante*  
*gobhyo devah samutthitah*  
*gobhir vedah samudgirnah*  
*sa-sad-anga-pada-kramah*

**“From cows come the Vedic sacrifices, and from cows arise the demigods. By cows all the Vedas, along with their six corollaries and word-by-word and permutated texts, have been uttered.”**

Krsna is anadi for the Yadus because they do not presume (adiyate) that He is their subordinate, and He is adi for the residents of Vraja because they do presume that He is their subordinate. Since this verse contains the phrase sarva-karana-karanam, “the cause of all causes,” anadir adir is not intended to mean that Krsna is without cause and is the cause of everything.

Calling Krsna “the cause of all causes” discloses another of His pastimes, the creation of the material world, which is enacted by His svamsa expansion, the Purusa.

Sri Caitanya-caritamrta (Madhya 20.165-66) records what Lord Caitanya Mahaprabhu taught Sanatana Gosvami about the Supreme Lords svayam-rupa.

The Supreme Lords ekatma forms are in essence identical with His svayam-rupa. Although there is no essential difference between Them, They appear different in Their bodily features and activities. The Visva-kosa dictionary defines akrti as akrtih kathita rupe samanya-vapusor api: “Akrti can be used to mean ‘form, ‘species,’ and ‘body.’”

They display potency nearly equal to that of the svayam-rupa. For example, Lord Narayana lacks only a few of Krsna’s unique qualities:

*madhurye venu-rupayoh*  
*ity asadharanam proktam*  
*govindasya catustayam*

**“His pastimes, His dear devotees who have exceptional love for Him, the charm of His flute, and His sweet beauty - these are the four unique qualities of Govinda.” (Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu 2.1.43)**

*parama-vyoma-nathas tu*  
*govindasya yatha smrtah*  
*parama-vyoma-nathasya*  
*vasudevas ca yadrsah*

**Пословный перевод:**

parama-vyoma — of the supreme sky (Vaikuntha); nathah— the Lord (Narayana); tu — and; govindasya — of Krsna; yatha —as; smrtah — is described in revealed scripture; parama-vyoma — of the supreme sky; nathasya — of the Lord; vasudevah — Vasudeva; ca — and; yadrsah — similar.

**For example, the scriptures describe the Lord of the spiritual sky, Narayana, as a vilasa of Govinda; and Lord Vasudeva, similarly, as a vilasa of Narayana.**

**Комментарий:**

The consensus of the Vedas is that all forms of Godhead and of the demigods expand from Krsna as their one original source. This is stated explicitly in such confidential texts as Sri Brahma-Samhita (5.43):

*goloka-namni nija-dhamni tale ca tasya*  
*devi-mahesa-hari-dhamasu tesu tesu*  
*te te prabhava-nicaya vihitas ca yena*  
*govindam adi-purusam tarn aham bhajami*

**“Below the planet named Goloka Vrndavana are the planets known as Devi- dhama, Mahesa-dhama, and Hari-dhama. These are opulent in different ways. I adore the primeval Lord Govinda, who has allotted the rulers of those graded realms their respective authorities.”**

Although Sri Krsna’s two expansions, Narayana and Vasudeva, seem the same in physical appearance, both having four arms and a dark blue complexion, They have different mentalities. As the subsequent expansion, Vasudeva considers Himself a servant of Narayana. He feels shy in the presence of Lord Narayana, just as Bharata feels constrained from acting independently from His elder brother Rama.

### Text 17

*svamsah,*  
*tadrso nyuma-saktim yo*  
*vyanakti svamsa iritah*  
*sankarsanadir matsyadir*  
*yatha tat-tat-sva-dhamasu*

**Пословный перевод:**

svamsah — the svamsa; tadrsah — such; ñóīñṁ — less; saktim — potency; yah — which; vyanakti — displays; svamsah—svamsa; iritah — is called; sankarsana-adih — Sahkarsana and so on; matsya-adih — Matsya and so on; yatha — as; tat tat — of each of Them; sva-dhamasu — in Their own abodes.

**Перевод:**

**The svamsa: That form similar to the vilasa expansions but displaying less potency is called svamsa. Among the svamsas are Sankarsana, Matsya, and others, each of whom appears in His own abode.**

**Комментарий:**

The svamsa expansions of Godhead, like the vilasa forms, are essentially nondifferent from the original svayam-rupa. In each of His personal forms God is never less than the complete whole, but the svamsa expansions may seem lesser because They refrain from exhibiting all of Their potencies.

Srlla Baladeva Vidyabhusana addresses a possible objection in this regard. Someone might suggest that distinguishing the forms of Godhead as amsa (part) and amsi (possessor of the part) goes against the teaching of our predecessor acarya, Sri Madhva Muni, in his explanation of the statement of the Vedanta-sutras (1.1.9), svapyayat. “his sutra literally means “because of merging back into Himself.” Sri Madhva explains it with the help of a verse found in both the Brhad-aranyaka Upanisad (5.1.1) and the Isa Upanisad (Invocation): îḍ ðīrnṁḍ adah ðīrnṁḍ idam / purnat ðīrnṁḍ udacyate. He asserts that all the avataras of the Supreme Person ultimately merge back into Him, their original source. According to the hypothetical presenter of this objection, then, since Acarya Madhva characterizes all the avataras of Godhead as ðīrnṁḍ (“complete”), there cannot be any distinction among them as amsa and amsi.

Srila Baladeva Vidyabhusana contends, on the contrary, that Madhva actually favors the concepts of amsa and amsi, as revealed by his comments on the section of the Vedanta-sutras beginning with sutrṁ 2.3.46, prakasadi- van naivam parah: “The Supreme is not like this, similar to light and so on.” According to Sri Madhva, although the avataras of God like Lord Matsya are amsas of the original amsi, they are not limited amsas like the jivas. He continues to explain that the Lords avataras and the jivas are similar in that they are both amsas, but there are important differences between them. One might also say that the fire of universal devastation and the illumination of a firefly are similar in that they are both expansions of the element fire, but they are very different. Similar comparisons could be made between urine and an ocean of nectar as products of the element water, and between feces and the great Mount Meru as products of the element earth. Despite their common origin, the members of each pair are very different from one another.

The purport of svapyayat, therefore, is not that there is no hierarchy of emanation among the forms of Godhead, but that the essential being of the

Supreme is always complete and perfect in all His appearances. Srila Rupa Gosvami will clarify this point in the fifth chapter of Laghu-bhagavatamrta (1.5.90):

*sakter vyaktis tathavyaktis*  
*taratamyasya karanam*

**“The manifestation or nonmanifestation of potency is the basis of gradation.”**

Sri Caitanya-caritamrta (Madhya 20.183-88) records Lord Caitanya Mahaprabhu's description of the Supreme Lords tad-ekatma-rupa in His teachings to Sanatana Gosvami.

### Text 22

*dvaravatyam yatha krsnah*  
*pratyaksam prati-mandiram*  
*citram bataitad ity-adi-*  
*pramanena sa setsyati*

**Пословный перевод:**

dvaravatyam — in Dvaraka; yatha — as; krsnah — Krsna; pratyaksam — visible; prati-mandiram — in each palace; citram — various; bata — indeed; etat — this; iti — thus saying; adi — and so on; pramanena — by the evidence; sah — it; setsyati — is demonstrated.

**Перевод:**

**For example, in Dvaraka Krsna was visible simultaneously in each of His palaces. This is confirmed by such statements as the one beginning “citram bataitat.”**

**Комментарий:**

The verse beginning citram bataitat was spoken by Narada Muni when He visited Krsna’s palaces in Dvaraka:

*citram bataitad ekena*  
*vapusa yugapat prthak*  
*grhesu dvy-asta-sahasram*  
*striya eka udavahat*

**“It is quite amazing that with a single body Lord Krsna simultaneously married sixteen thousand women, each in a separate palace.” (Bhagavatam 10.69.2)**

We find in various scriptures that Krsna expands Himself to appear at the same time in the forest groves of Candravali, Radhika, and other gopis, or in the palaces of Rukmini, Satyabhama, and other queens. We might ask which of His forms are the amsas and which form is the amsi? The current verses address this question. The Lord’s prakasa forms are not included in the vilasa or svamsa categories because They do not manifest different qualities. Thus when Krsna goes out from the palaces of Nanda Maharaja or Vasudeva and simultaneously enters the residences of several of His beloveds in Vraja or Dvaraka, manifesting the very same form in more than one location, these are called His prakasa expansions. His prakasa is not different from Himself in bodily appearance, qualities, and style of pastimes.

This verse mentions Krsna’s prakasa expansions in Dvaraka, but He had also exhibited His prakasa expansions in Vraja during the rasa-lila:

*krtva tavantam atmanam*  
*yavatir gopa-yositah*  
*reme sa bhagavams tabhir*  
*atmaramo ’pi lilaya*

**“Expanding Himself as many times as there were cowherd women to associate with, the Supreme Lord, though self-satisfied, playfully enjoyed their company.” (Bhagavatam 10.33.19)**

The word krtva in this Tenth Canto verse should not be understood in the sense of “creating”; rather Krsna “manifested” His eternally existing form by the side of each gopi.

Krsna's being “self-satisfied” in Vraja means that He is always satisfied in relationships with the manifestations of His transcendental energy, which are nondifferent from Himself.

### Text 23

*kvacic catur-bhujatve ’pi*  
*na tyajet krsna-rupatam*  
*atah prakasa eva syat*  
*tasyasau dvi-bhujasya ca*

**Пословный перевод:**

kvacit — sometimes; catuh-bhujatve — while having four arms; api — even; na tyajet —He does not give up; krsna-rupatam — His identity as Krsna; atah — thus; prakasah— a prakasa expansion; eva — indeed; syat — is; tasya — His; asau — this; dvi-bhujasya — of Him with two arms; ca — and.

**Перевод:**

**Sometimes Krsna does not give up His original character even when He appears with four arms. Thus some four-armed forms are prakasa expansions of the two-armed Lord.**

**Комментарий:**

When Krsna was consoling Rukmini after teasing her with the idea that she ought to select another, better husband, He stood before her with four arms instead of two. Should this form Krsna manifested in Dvaraka be counted as a vilasa-rupa, since it is different from His original form? No, Krsna remains the same even when He sometimes assumes an extra two arms for certain pastimes in Vrndavana, Mathura, or Dvaraka.

In this verse krsna-rupatam means “the original character of Krsna, who drank from Mother Yasoda’s breast.” Rupa can also mean “character,” according to the Medini-kosa dictionary: rupam svabhave saundarye: “Rupa can be used to mean character' and ‘beauty.”’

The original form of Krsna has two arms like an ordinary human being: yatravatirnah krsnakhyam param brahma narakrti. “Where the Supreme Absolute Truth descended in human form with the name Krsna.” (Visnu Purana 4.11.2) Occasionally He shows four arms in situations eliciting moods like humor, without losing His primary identity. For example, this is how we can understand Krsna’s appearance before His parents with four arms at His birth. Sukadeva Gosvami states, babhuva prakrtah sisuh (Bhagavatam 10.3.46), “He became a regular baby,” indicating that by changing from His four-armed form to His two-armed baby form Krsna merely displayed His original nature.

The Upanisads also confirm that Krsna’s real identity is two-armed:

*sat-pundarika-nayanam meghabham vaidyutambaram*  
*dvi-bhujam mauna-mudradhyam vana-malinam isvaram*

**“That Lord has two arms, eyes like beautiful lotuses, and a complexion the color of a rain cloud. He wears clothing the color of lightning, displays the gestures of a sage, and sports a garland of forest flowers.” (Gopala-tapani Upanisad, Purva 10)**

One should not think that Krsna’s form with four arms is superior to His form with only two, since this idea disagrees with the Anandakhya-samhita:

*sthulam asta-bhujam proktam*  
*suksmam caiva catur-bhujam*  
*param tu dvi-bhujam proktam*  
*tasmad etat trayam yajet*

**“His eight-armed form is said to be bulky, while His four-armed form is considered subtle. The supreme form, however, is said to be the two-armed form. Therefore one should worship all three of these.”**

The Samhita advises us to worship all three forms because they are essentially nondifferent. Nonetheless, the Gopala-tapani Upanisad relates that Lord Brahma obtained the power to create the universe by meditating on Krsna’s two-armed form.

Srila Krsnadasa Kaviraja also describes the Lords prakasa forms in Sri Caitanya-caritamrta (Adi 1.68-75 and Madhya 20.166-83).

**This ends the examination of the categories of Godhead in terms of svayam-rupa, vilasa, svamsa, avesa, and prakasa.**

Every one of the Supreme Lords personal expansions is eternal, and each has His own eternal abode in the spiritual world. That the residences of the Godheads expansions are all eternal is declared in many scriptures:

**“All the abodes in which the Supreme Lord takes delight on the earth are present in Vaikuntha. He honors each of them with various pastimes.” (Skanda Purana)**

*nivasanti mahojjvalah*  
*avatarah sada tatra*  
*matsya-kurmadayo 'khilah*

**“All the Lords supremely resplendent avataras - Matsya, Kurma, and the others - reside always in that eternal world of Vaikuntha.” (Padma Purana)**

## Chapter 2 - Purusa-avataras and Guna-avataras

### Text 1

*athavatarah kathyante*  
*krsno yesu ca puskalah*

**Пословный перевод:**

atha — next; avatarah— the avataras; kathyante — are discussed; krsnah — Krsna; yesu — among whom; ca — and; puskalah — the most complete.

**Перевод:**

**Next comes a discussion of the Lord’s avataras, among whom Krsna is the most complete.**

**Комментарий:**

By calling Krsna “the original Personality of Godhead” (bhagavan svayam), Srimad-Bhagavatam indicates that He is the source of all the avataras of Godhead. The next topic is the avataras who expand from Krsna. But isn’t Krsna Himself said to be one of the avataras? Yes, in the context of making a list of avataras it is convenient to list Him among the others, but He is puskala, “the most complete.” He is the original svayam-rupa. According to the Haima dictionary, puskalas tu purane sresthe: “Puskala means complete or ‘best.”’

### Text 2

*tal-laksanam,*  
*purvokta visva-karyartham*  
*apurva iva cet svayam*  
*dvarantarena vavihsyur*  
*avataras tada stutah*

**Пословный перевод:**

tat — of Them; laksanam — the definition; purva-ukta — described above; visva — in the material creation; karya-artham — for purposes; apurvah — unprecedented; iva — as if; cet — if; svayam — by Themselves; dvara- antarena — through an agency; va — or; avihsyuh — They become manifest; avatarah — avataras; tada — then; stutah — called.

**Перевод:**

**Here is the definition of avatara: When the above-mentioned forms of the Lord appear unprecedentedly for various purposes in the material creation, either solely by Their own power or through some agency, they are called avataras.**

**Комментарий:**

The first chapter of this book defined the major categories of the Supreme Persons expansions. The forms of Godhead in each of the categories described there become avataras when They descend from the spiritual to the material world. Avataras can appear through parents, as expansions, or without the help of any agency. Among those who appear through parents are Lords Krsna and Ramacandra, the sons of Vasudeva and Dasaratha, respectively. Among those who appear as expansions is Garbhodaka-sayi Visnu, who expands from Sesa-sayi Maha-visnu in the Causal Ocean. And among those who appear without help are Matsya and Hamsa.

The various purposes of the Supreme Lords avataras can be summarized generally as visva-karya, creating the universe and helping its inhabitants. Maha-visnu, for example, agitates primordial nature with His glance and stimulates her to evolve the causal elements. Other avataras subdue malefactors for the relief of the demigods and other faithful servants of the Lord. Others bestow upon the eager seekers of truth the greatest benefits by revealing Themselves, by teaching the principles of pure devotional service, and by granting the bliss of love of God.

Although the Supreme Lords forms exist eternally, as avataras They dramatically appear in the material world as if novel creations of the times and places of Their advent.

*tac ca dvaram tad-ekatma-*  
*rupas tad-bhakta eva ca*  
*sesa-sayyadiko yadvad*  
*vasudevadiko 'pi ca*

**Пословный перевод:**

tat — that; ca — and; dvaram — agency; tat-eka-atma-rupah — a tad-ekatma form; tat — His; bhaktah — a devotee; eva — — indeed; ca — and; sesa — on Sesa; sayi — lying; adikah — and so on; yadvat — as; Vasudeva — Vasudeva; adikah — and so on; api ca — also.

**Перевод:**

**The agent through whom an avatara appears can be a tad-ekatma form of the Lord, such as He who lies on Sesa Naga, or a devotee of the Lord, like Vasudeva.**

**Пословный перевод:**

**Перевод:**

**The Lord's avataras are of three kinds: the Purusas, those who preside over the modes of nature, and those who appear in order to perform pastimes.**

**Комментарий:**

Lord Caitanya explained these divisions of avataras in His instructions to Sanatana Gosvami (Caitanya-caritamrta, Madhya 20.244-46).

### Text 5

*prayah svamsas tathavesa*  
*avatara bhavanty ami*  
*atra yah syat svayam-rupah*  
*so 'gre vyakti-bhavisyati*

**Пословный перевод:**

prayah — mostly; svamsah— svamsa forms; tatha — also; avesah— avesa forms; avatarah — avataras; bhavanti — are; ami— these; atra — in this book; yah — which; syat — is; svayam-rupah — a svayam-rupa form; sah — that; agre — later; vyakti-bhavisyati — will be revealed.

**Перевод:**

**Most of these avataras are either svamsa or avesa expansions. The one avatara who is svayam-rupa will be discussed later on.**

**Комментарий:**

Maha-visnu is an example of a svamsa avatara. The four Kumaras and Prthu are avesa avataras. This verse qualifies its first assertion with the word prayah (“for the most part”), because sometimes the svayam-rupa}the origin of all other forms of God, descends to the material world. That most special of avataras will be discussed at length in the fifth chapter of Sri Laghṝ - bhagavatamrta.

### Text 6

*tatra purusa-laksanam, yatha visnu-purane,*  
*tasyaiva yo 'nu guna-bhug bahudhaika eva*  
*suddho 'py asuddha iva murti-vibhaga-bhedaih*  
*jnananvitah sakala-sattva-vibhuti-karta*  
*tasmai nato 'smi purusaya sadavyayaya*  
*tasyaiva anu purvoktat paramesvara samanantaram iti svami.*

**Пословный перевод:**

tatra — among them; purusa— of the Purusa; laksanam — the characteristics; yatha — as; visnu-purane — in the Visnu Purana; tasya — His; eva — just; yah — which; anu — subsequently; guna-bhuk— associating with the material modes; bahudha — manifold; ekah — one; eva — only; suddhah — pure; api — although; asuddhah — impure; iva — as if; murti-vibhaga— of separate forms; bhedaih — with the differences; jnana-anvitah — endowed with knowledge; sakala — all; sattva — of pure goodness; vibhuti — the wonders; karta — who creates; tasmai — unto Him; natah — bowed down; asmi — I am; purusaya — to the Purusa; sada — always; avyayaya — who is infallible; tasya — His; eva — only; anu — following; purva-uktat — who was previously described; parama-isvarat — to the Supreme Personality of Godhead; samanantaram — subsequent; iti — thus; svami — Sridhara Svami.

**Перевод:**

**Among the three kinds of avataras, the Purusa avatara is described as follows in the Visnu Purana s6.8.61\]: “I how down to the always infallible Purusa, who appears from the original Supreme Lord. The Purusa is completely transcendental, although He seems otherwise when He expands Himself into various personal forms who associate with the modes of material nature. He possesses perfect knowledge and manifests all the living beings in the wonderful material creation.” Srila Sridhara Svami comments that “tasyaiva anu,” “He appears afterwards,” indicates that He expands from the Supreme Personality of Godhead who had been previously described.**

**Комментарий:**

As indicated by the word anu in this verse of the Visnu Purana, the Purusa avatara expands from the original Godhead, who was glorified a few verses earlier:

*nanto 'sti yasya na ca yasya samudbhavo 'sti*  
*vrddhir na yasya parinama-vivarjitasya*  
*napaksayam ca samupaity avikalpa-vastu*  
*yas tam nato 'smi purusottamam adyarn idyam*

**“I bow down to Him who has no end and no birth, who does not develop or change, and who never suffers decay. He is the immutable reality, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the original, worshipable Lord.” (Visnu Purana 6.8.58)**

The Purusa associates with material nature only to the extent of glancing at prakrti at the beginning of creation and maintaining conscious control over the creation that evolves from her. He never gives up His unity, even while expanding into numerous amsa forms. He generates the wonderful cosmos, filling it with all sorts of living beings.

Does this mean that the Purusa becomes affected by contact with nature and her creation? No. Because the entire process of creation is set into motion simply by His desire, prakrti cannot affect Him. Even while the material world is being conducted by His prakrti, He remains uninfluenced, thanks to His inconceivable personal energies.

### Text 7

*atra karika,*  
*paramesamsa-rupo yah*  
*pradhana-guna-bhag iva*  
*tad iksadi-krtir nana-*  
*vatarah purusah smrtah*

**Пословный перевод:**

atra — in this regard; karika —an explanatory verse; parama-isa — of the Supreme Godhead; amsa-rupah — appearing as a partial manifestation; yah — who; pradhana — of primeval nature; guna — the qualities; bhak — partaking of; iva — as if; tat — upon her; iksa— glance; adi— and so on; krtih— doing; ñṁñṁ — many; avatarah— having incarnations; purusah — the Purusa; smrtah — is described.

**Перевод:**

**Here is an explanatory verse:**

**Scripture describes the Purusa as the partial expansion of the Supreme Personality of Godhead who seems to connect with the qualities of material nature, beginning with making the effort to glance at her, and who has many incarnations.**

**Комментарий:**

Srila Rupa Gosvami presents the Laghu-bhagavatamrta in the typically concise style of philosophical Sastras. Short definitions and statements of fact with the support of quotations from authoritative scriptures, which are then often followed by the authors own karikas, or explanatory verses. Karika yatana-vrttyoh: “The word karika can mean ‘torment’ or commentary on a basic text.’” (Amara-kosa)

Texts 6 and 7 apply to all three of the Purusa incarnations. We also find general information about the purusa-avataras in Lord Caitanya's instructions to Sanatana Gosvami (Caitanya-caritamrta, Madhya 20.250-64).

**Пословный перевод:**

**Перевод:**

**That He is an avatara is confirmed in the Second Canto of Srimad-Bhagavatam s2.6.42\]: “The Purusa is the first incarnation of the Supreme Lord.”**

**Комментарий:**

The first Purusa, Karanarnava-sayi Visnu (Maha-visnu), is an incarnation of Krsna, the ultimate avatari.

He who knows these three becomes liberated from the clutches of maya.”**

In this verse visnu refers to the original Supreme Lord, the svayam-rupa. The first Purusa, Sankarsana, is the Supersoul of prakrti; the second, Pradyumna, is the Supersoul of four-headed Brahma; and the third, Aniruddha, is the Supersoul of each of the jivas.

**Комментарий:**

The supremely independent Lord of Vaikuntha, Sri Narayana, expanded Himself as Sankarsana, the first Purusa, who produced from His own body the five elements of creation, from which He fashioned the egg-like universes. He then entered each egg as Pradyumna, the second Purusa.

From that eternal person has sprung the vast expanse of spiritual water, the Causal Ocean, which is the subjective portion of Sankarsana, who abides in the para-vyoma. The above-mentioned supreme Purusa, Maha-visnu, with thousands of subjective portions, reposes in the state of divine sleep syoga-nidra\] in the waters of the Causal Ocean”**

*tad-roma-bila-jalesu*

**Перевод:**

**Maha-visnu originates as an expansion of Narayana, the Lord of Vaikuntha, who is a partial expansion (linga) of the svayam-rupa Personality of Godhead, Krsna. Maha-visnu appears “within” Narayana, or more exactly near Him, in one corner of His Vaikuntha realm. He “became manifest” (avirabhut) in the sense of making His appearance in the Causal Ocean to glance at prakrti.**

**Комментарий:**

To dispel any doubts that Maha-visnu is certainly that expansion of Narayana whose acts of creation are described in the Visnu Purana (1.4.6), it is mentioned here that the waters of creation emanate from Him.

*apo tiara iti prokta*  
*apo vai nara-sunavah*  
*ayanam tasya tah purvam*  
*tena narayanah smrtah*

**“The water from which the material creation evolves is called nara because it is born from Nara, the Supreme Person. Because that Supreme Person is the primeval origin of these waters, the scriptures remember Him as Narayana.”**

Since the water of the Causal Ocean is produced from the body of Sankarsana Maha-visnu, it is termed sankarsanatmaka. Lord Maha-visnu lies down on that ocean, resting on the bed of Ananta Sesa. Therefore He is called Karanarnava-sayi. He glances at material nature, thus impregnating her with the seeds of the universes and the spiritual sparks who will populate those universes. Germinating within the womb of prakrti, the seedlike universes develop into golden eggs. Lord Maha-visnu then expands Himself thousands of times - or rather, countless times - as the Pradyumna Garbhodaka-sayi Visnus in all the universal eggs.

### Text 12

*lirigam atra svayam-rupa-*

**The word “lingam” sin Brahma-samhita 5.10, quoted above\] indicates a particular expansion of the original svayarii-rupa Lord.**

Srlla Krsnadasa Kaviraja writes about the first Purusa incarnation in the Caitanya-caritamrta, at Adi-lila 5.50-91 and 6.13-19, and also at Madhya-lila 20.265-82, where he describes Lord Caitanyas instructions to Sanatana Gosvami.

Srimad-Bhagavatam 1.3.1 also depicts Lord Maha-visnu:

*jagrhe paurusam rupam*  
*bhagavan mahad-adibhih*  
*sambhutam sodasa-kalam*  
*adau loka-sisrksaya*

**“In the beginning of the creation, the Lord first expanded Himself in the universal form of the Purusa incarnation and manifested all the ingredients for the material creation. And thus at first there was the creation of the sixteen principles of material action. This was for the purpose of creating the material universe.”**

And Srila Sanatana Gosvams Brhad-bhagavatamrta, second part (3.33-46), describes Maha-visnus expansion as Lord Mahakala, who resides beyond the universes outer shell of pradhana.

*ekamsad visati svayam*  
*iti.*

**Пословный перевод:**

Here evam means “in this way,” or in other words in the same transcendental way that He glances at prakrti, impregnating her without becoming at all entangled. Maha-visnu enters each universe in a separate form as the second Purusa. Some manuscripts of the Brahma-samhita record praty- andam (“each egg”) for this verse instead of praty-ekam (“each one”), but this creates no real difference in meaning.

### Text 14

*garbhodaka-sayah padma-*  
*nabho sav aniruddhakah*  
*iti narayanopakhya-*  
*na uktam moksa-dharmake*  
*so yam hiranyagarbhasya*  
*pradyumnatve niyamakah*

**Пословный перевод:**

garbha-udaka — in the Garbha Ocean; sayah — lying; padma-nabhah — Lord Padmanabha; asau — He; aniruddhakah — as Aniruddha; iti — thus called; narayana— about Narayana; upṁkhyane — in the narration; uktam — referred to; moksa-dharmake— in the Moksa-dharma; sah— He; ayam — this; hiranya-garbhasya — of Hiranyagarbha; pradyumnatve—as Pradyumna; niyamakah — the controller.

**In the Narayaniya section of the Moksa-dharma Lord Padmanabha, who lies on the Garbha Ocean, is called Aniruddha. This same Garbhodaka-sayi Visnu, as Pradyumna, is the controller of Hiranya-garbha Brahma.**

**Комментарий:**

Strictly speaking, from the catur-vyuha in Vaikuntha, the first Visnu Purusa expands from Sankarsana, the second from Pradyumna, and the third from Aniruddha; yet sometimes these names are used freely for any or all of the three. They are all forms of the same Supreme Person.

We should thus not fault the Narayaniya narration in the Mahabharata (Santi-parva 236.68-69, 327.26) for referring to Garbhodaka-sayi, the progenitor of Brahma, as Aniruddha:

*asman-murtis caturthi ya*  
*sasrjac chesam avyayam*  
*sa hi sankarsanah proktah*  
*pradyumnam so ’py ajijanat*  
*pradyumnac caniruddho 'hath*  
*sargo mama punah punah*  
*aniruddhat tato brahma*  
*tan-nabhi-kamalodbhavah*

**“My fourth personal form generated His infallible expansion known as Sankarsana. Sankarsana further expanded as Pradyumna, and from Pradyumna came Aniruddha. Thus I expanded Myself again and again. Brahma came from Aniruddha, appearing on the lotus growing from His navel.”**

*aniruddho hi lokanam*  
*mahan atmeti kathyate*  
*yo sau vyaktatvam apanno*  
*nirmame ca pitamaham*

**“Aniruddha is known as the Supreme Soul of all the worlds. Assuming the manifest form of the universal body, He gave birth to Brahma, the forefather of all beings” (Mahabharata, Santi-parva 339.70-72, 340.27-28)**

Srimad-Bhagavatam 1.3.2-3 specifies that Brahma appears on the lotus growing from the second Purusa:

*yasyambhasi sayanasya*  
*yoga-nidram vitanvatah*  
*nabhi-hradambujad asid*  
*brahma visva-srjam patih*  
*yasyavayava-samsthanaih*  
*kalpito loka-vistarah*  
*tad vai bhagavato rupam*  
*visuddham sattvam urjitam*

**“A part of the Purusa lies down within the water of the universe, from the navel lake of His body sprouts a lotus stem, and from the lotus flower atop this stem Brahma, the master of all engineers in the universe, becomes manifest. It is believed that all the universal planetary systems arc situated on the extensive body of the Purusa, but He has nothing to do with the created material ingredients. His body is eternally in spiritual existence par excellence.”**

These two verses of the Bhagavatam indicate that since the Supreme Lord never actually has a material body, conceiving of the universal form as the body of God helps materialistic persons purify their intelligence. The universal form is not Garbhodaka-sayi Visnus body but Brahmas. It is subtler than the four-headed body Brahma later acquires, and it is sometimes called Hiranyagarbha. The Purusas own body, on the other hand, is visuddham sattvam, pure spirit, and urjitam, innately endowed with self-manifested, unlimited consciousness. Appearing in His perfect, incorruptible body within the universe, the second Purusa gives birth to Hiranyagarbha Brahma. Then, as the Supersoul within that universal body, the Lord guides Brahma.

The Garbhodaka-sayl Purusa is described in some detail in Sri Caitanya- caritamrta (Adi 5.93-107 and Madhya 20.283-93).

The virat-rupa expansion from the second Purusa is explained in several chapters of Srimad-Bhagavatam, including chapter six of the Second Canto.

Lord Maha-visnus appearance as the Maha-purusa incarnation on Brahmaloka is described by Srila Sanatana Gosvami in Sri Brhad- bhagavatamrta (first part, chapter two, texts 34, 39-42, and 50-52; and second part, chapter two, texts 130-32,141-43, and 226-28).

In the second chapter of the Second Canto of Srimad-Bhagavatam, Suka- deva Gosvami briefly describes how to meditate on the Supersoul present in ones own heart:

*kecit sva-dehantar-hrdayavakase*  
*pradesa-matram purusam vasantam*  
*catur-bhujam kanja-rathanga-sankha-*  
*gada-dharam dharanaya smaranti*

**“Others conceive of the Personality of Godhead residing within the body in the region of the heart and measuring only eight inches, with four hands carrying a lotus, a wheel of a chariot, a conch shell, and a club, respectively.” (Bhagavatam 2.2.8)**

As Srila Sukadeva reveals in this verse and subsequent verses, the third Purusa, the Lord of the Milk Ocean, enters the heart of every living being in the appropriate size. In the case of human beings, Lord Ksirodaka-sayi Visnus form is the height of one pradesa, the distance between the tips of a persons extended thumb and index finger.

The third Purusa is also described in Sri Caitanya-caritamrta (Adi 5.109-116 and Madhya 20.294-95).

### Text 16

**Next, the guna-avataras: The guna incarnations are said to appear from the Purusa as Visnu, Brahma, and Rudra for the purposes of maintenance, creation, and destruction, respectively.**

These three avataras appear from the Supreme Lords second Purusa form.

### Text 17

*yatha prathame —*  
*sattvam rajas tama iti prakrter gunas tair*

*sreyamsi tatra khalu sattva-tanor nrnam syuh*  
*iti.*

**Пословный перевод:**

yatha —as; prathame — in the First Canto; sattvam — goodness; rajah — passion; tamah — the darkness of ignorance; iti — thus; prakrteh — of material nature; gunah — the qualities; taih — with them; yuktah — associated; parah — transcendental; purusah — the personality; ekah — one; iha — here; asya — of this material world; dhatte — accepts; sthiti-adaye — for the matter of creation, maintenance, and destruction, etc.; hari — Visnu, the Personality of Godhead; virihci— Brahma; hara — Lord Siva; iti — thus; samjnah — names; sreyamsi — ultimate benefits; tatra — among these; khalu — of course; sattva — of goodness; tanoh— from the form; nrnam— for human beings; syuh — are derived; iti — thus.

**As is stated in the First Canto s1.2.23\]: “The transcendental Personality of Godhead is indirectly associated with the three modes of material nature, namely passion, goodness, and ignorance, and just for the material world’s creation, maintenance, and destruction He accepts the three qualitative forms of Brahma, Visnu, and Siva, respectively. Of these three, all human beings can derive ultimate benefit from Visnu, the form of the quality of goodness”**

**Комментарий:**

This transcendental Personality of Godhead” is Garbhodaka-sayi Visnu, who expands Himself separately as each of the three guna-avataras.

The fourfold goals of human life - religiosity, economic success, sense gratification, and liberation - can be fully realized only by worshiping the avatara of the mode of goodness, Visnu.

### Text 18

*tatra karika,*  
*yogo niyamakataya*  
*gunaih sambandha ucyate*  
*atah sa tair na yujyeta*  
*tatra svamsah parasya yah*

**Пословный перевод:**

tatra — in that regard; karika — a karika; yogah — association; niyamakataya — as the controller; gunaih — with the modes of nature; sambandhah — connection; ucyate — is called; atah — thus; sah — His; taih — with those (modes); na yujyeta —does not join; tatra — there; sva- arhsah — a svamsa expansion; parasya — of the Supreme; yah — which.

**Перевод:**

**The “association” mentioned here refers to a connection with the modes of nature as their controller. Thus, the particular guna-avatara who is a svamsa of the Supreme Lord does not actually contact the material modes.**

**Комментарий:**

How can the Supreme Person have a connection with the modes of material nature? Indeed, according to Srimad-Bhagavatam 2.7.47, just the opposite is the case: maya paraity abhimukhe ca vilajjamana, “Maya stays far away from Him, ashamed to show herself to His face.”

Yes, this is true, but as explained here, the yoga or ‘connection” of the Supreme Lord with the material modes is not like that of the finite living beings, who become entangled when they consort with these modes. The three gunas remain subordinate to the Personality of Godheads three guna- avataras, who regulate the modes’ control of the material world.

In particular, Lord Visnu can never come under the sway of prakrti and her modes.

*adav abhuc chata-dhrti rajasasya sarge*  
*visnuh sthitau kratu-patir dvija-dharma-setuh*  
*rudro ’pyayaya tamasa purusah sa adya*  
*ity udbhava-sthiti-layah satatam prajasu*

**“First, the original Supreme Personality manifested the form of Brahma through the material mode of passion in order to create this universe. Then the Lord manifested His form as Visnu, the Lord of sacrifice and the protector of the brahmanas and their religious duties, to maintain the universe. And when the universe is to be annihilated, the same Supreme Lord employs the material mode of ignorance and manifests the form of Rudra. The created living beings are thus always subject to the forces of creation, maintenance, and destruction.” (Bhagavatam 11.4.5)**

In this verse the great yoga master Drumila describes Brahma as connected with the mode of passion and Siva as connected with ignorance, but he describes Visnu without any mention of a connection to goodness or the other material modes.

The guna-avatara Visnu is a svamsa expansion of Godhead, always situated in transcendence, free from all coverings of false material identity. But when the Supreme Lord chooses to associate with the modes of passion and ignorance, He becomes Brahma and Siva. Similarly, when He chooses to associate with atheism, He becomes Buddha, and in association with deviant behavior He becomes Rsabha. In reality, however, the Supreme Lord is never contaminated by the material modes.

However, worshiping the Supreme Lord disguised as Brahma or Siva cannot bring about full realization of dharma, artha and kama. And it certainly cannot lead to moksa. As Lord Siva says in the Hari-vamsa, mukti- pradata sarvesam visnur eva na samsayah: “Lord Visnu is undoubtedly the only bestower of liberation for everyone.” The material mode of goodness has no power over Lord Visnu. He is not in direct contact with it but controls it merely by His desire. Therefore real benefit comes only from worshiping Him directly.

In the words of the Vamana Purana:

*brahma-visnv-isa-rupani*  
*trini visnor mahatmanah*  
*brahmani brahma-rupah sa*  
*siva-rupah sive sthitah*  
*prthag eva sthito deva*  
*visnu-rupi janardanah*

**“Brahma, Visnu, and Isa are three forms of the Supreme Soul Visnu. Lord Janardana situates His Brahma form in Lord Brahma and His Siva form in Lord Siva. The same Supreme Lord, however, remains Himself in His Visnu form”**

I he ruler of all three modes of nature is indeed the one Supreme Lord, but He expands Himself as each of the guna-avataras.

Contact with the mode of goodness is more beneficial than contact with passion and ignorance. The Bhagavatam verse that follows the one quoted in text 17 confirms this:

*parthivad daruno dhumas*  
*tasmad agnis trayi-mayah*  
*tamasas tu rajas tasmat*  
*sattvam yad brahma-darsanam*

**“Firewood is a transformation of earth, but smoke is better than the raw wood. And fire is still better, for by fire we can derive the benefits of superior knowledge sthrough Vedic sacrifices\]. Similarly, passion is better than ignorance, but goodness is still better, for by goodness we can come to realize the Absolute Truth.” (Bhagavatam 1.2.24)**

Firewood, smoke, and fire are respectively ineffective, imperfectly effective, and fully effective for executing Vedic sacrifice. Similarly, the modes of tamas, rajas, and sattva – with their bewildering, agitating, and enlightening influences - respectively block realization, allow partial realization, and facilitate full realization of the Supreme Truth. It is therefore appropriate to say that the Personality of Godhead in His expansions as the controllers of tamas and rajas does not bestow genuine success, but that He does bestow this success in His role as the controller of sattva-guna.

### Text 19

*tatra brahma,*  
*hiranyagarbhah suksmo ’tra*  
*sthulo vairaja-samjhakah*  
*bhogaya srstaye cabhut*  
*padma-bhur iti sa dvidha*

**Пословный перевод:**

tatra — there; brahma — Brahma; hiranyagarbhah — Hiranyagarbha; suksmah — subtle; atra — here; sthulah — gross; vairaja — Vairaja (the universal form); samjhakah — called; bhogaya — for enjoyment; srstaye — for creation; ca — and; abhut — came into being; padma-bhuh — born from the lotus; iti — thus; sah — he; dvidha — in two ways.

**Перевод:**

**Regarding Brahma: In this world his subtle form is known as Hiranya- garbha and his gross form as Vairaja, and he also appears as the lotus-born one (Padmabhu). He accepts these forms for furthering his enjoyment and for creating the universe.**

**He appears in two different ways, as follows.**

**Комментарий:**

The Personality of Godhead Himself sometimes plays Brahmas role, and sometimes He empowers a jiva for this purpose. The previous verses described the first case, and now the second is being considered. Hiranyagarbha is the name for Brahma in his subtle body, the mahat-tattva.

Only the Supreme Lord can see him in that form, the demigods cannot. Vairaja is the name for Brahma in his grosser universal body; many yogis meditate on this form. His third body, with four heads, eight eyes, and eight arms, can be seen by the demigods and other living beings, who can then receive benedictions from him.

His first purpose for appearing in these forms is his own enjoyment, and his second purpose is to create the universe. He also has another responsibility, implied by the word ca: to promulgate the Vedas. We read in the Kurma Purana: veda-pracaranarthaya brahma jatas catur-mukhah: “Fourheaded Brahma was born to disseminate the Vedas.”

### Text 22

*visnur yatra maha-kalpe*  
*srastrtvam ca prapadyate*  
*tatra bhuhkte tarn pravisya*  
*vairdjah saukhya-sampadam*  
*ato jivatvam aisyam ca*  
*brahmanah kala-bhedatah*

**Пословный перевод:**

visnuh— Visnu; yatra — in which; maha-kalpe— cycle of creation; srastr- tvam— the role of creator; ca — and; prapadyate — assumes; tatra — then; bhunkte — enjoys; tam — Him; pravisya— entering; vairajah— known as Vairaja; saukhya — for happiness; sampadam — the facilities; atah — thus; jivatvam — identity as a jiva; aisyam — identity as God; ca —and; brahmanah — Brahma; kala-bhedatah — according to different times.

**Перевод:**

**During a maha-kalpa in which Visnu becomes the creator, Vairaja Brahma enters within Him and enjoys all facilities for material happiness.**

**Thus Brahma is sometimes a jiva and sometimes the Supreme Lord.**

**Комментарий:**

In the kalpas when Visnu Himself becomes Brahma, what does the jiva Brahma do? Does he achieve liberation at the very beginning of his life? No. Brahma can be liberated only after living out his lifespan of one hundred years. As Dvaipayana Vyasa states in the Vedanta-sutras (3.3.33), yavad adhikaram avasthitir adhikarikanam: “The appointed administrative demigods must remain in their posts for the duration of their terms.”

This verse answers the question posed above: In kalpas when Visnu is Brahma, the jiva Brahma enters the spiritual body of Visnu with both his Vairaja body and his subtle Hiranyagarbha body. This jiva Brahma thus enjoys the offerings the demigods make in his name. Just see the generosity of the Supreme Lord in granting His servant the ability to enjoy the advantages of his position without having to take any responsibility!

Thus the role of Brahma can be taken by either a jiva or God.

### Text 23

*isatvapeksaya tasya*  
*sastre proktavatarata*  
*samastitvena bhagavat-*  
*sannikrstatayocyate*  
*asyavatarata kaiscid*  
*avesatvena kaiscana*

**Пословный перевод:**

isatva— the position of God; apeksaya— in regards to; tasya — his (Brahmas); sastre—in revealed scripture; prokta— is stated; avatarata — the identity as an avatara; samastitvena — as the collective body; bhagavat— to the Personality of Godhead; sannikrstataya — because of being very close; ucyate — is said; asya — His; avatdratd — being an incarnation; kaiscit— by some; dvesatvena — because of being an avesa form; kaiscana — by some.

**Перевод:**

**The revealed scriptures speak of Brahma as an avatara because his form comes directly from the Supreme Lord. Other authorities say he is an incarnation because of how intimate he becomes with the Personality of Godhead while ruling the universal body. Still others describe him as an avesa incarnation.**

**Комментарий:**

There are various opinions as to why Brahma is called an avatara. In the most complete sense he is considered an incarnation because he appears directly from Lord Garbhodaka-sayi Visnu.

Some Vaisnava acaryas consider Brahma an avatara because of his close association with Lord Visnu in sharing the virat form with Him. Garbhodaka-sayi Visnu embraces Brahmas universal body infusing it with the potencies of creation. The finite soul Brahma and Supersoul Visnu retain their separate identities, but the two become intimately associated, like a mixture of water and milk.

Other acaryas explain that Brahma is an avesa incarnation like certain other jivas.

In any case, when the Supreme Lord rather than an appointed jiva is playing the role of Brahma, he is more fully an avatara.

This verse of Brahma-samhita describes how a jiva with exceptional karma is empowered to take birth with the whole universe as his body and to use that universal form to create the various worlds and the individual bodies that inhabit them. Such empowerment is further explained below, in the discussion of the third guna-avatara, Rudra.

### Text 25

*garbhoda-sayino syabhut*  
*janma nabhi-saroruhat*  
*kadacit sruyate nirat*  
*tejo-vatadikad api*

**Пословный перевод:**

garbha-uda-sayinah— of Garbhoda-sayi Visnu; asya — his; abhut— came about; janma — birth; nabhi — of the navel; saroruhat— from the lotus; kadacit — sometimes; sruyate — is known; nirat — from the water; tejah— fire; vata— wind; adikat — and from other causes; api — also.

**Brahma is born from the lotus growing from the navel of Garbhoda-sayi Visnu. But the scriptures say that sometimes he is born from the Garbha water itself or from another source, such as fire or wind.**

**Комментарий:**

As the Supreme Lord wills, from time to time Brahma may appear in ways other than from the lotus sprouting from the Lords own navel.

Srila Sanatana Gosvami reveals the glories of Lord Brahma in the Brhad-bhagavatamrta (1.2.30-79 and 2.2.121-129).

Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami gives a description of Brahma as a guna- avatara in the Caitanya-caritamrta (Madhya 20.302-5).

Srimad-Bhagavatam presents a condensed account of the Bhagavatam that Brahma presented to his son Narada (Second Canto, chapters 5-7). The Bhagavatam also describes Brahmas performance of austerities under the guidance of Garbhodaka-sayi Visnu and his subsequent vision of Vaikuntha (2.9.4-39). And the Bhagavatam relates how Brahma created the material universe (Third Canto, chapters 8-12).

### Text 26

*sri-rudrahy*  
*rudra ekadasa-vyuhas*  
*tathasta-tanur apy asau*  
*prayah pahcananas try-akso*  
*dasa-bahur udiryate*

**Пословный перевод:**

sri-rudrah— Sri Rudra; rudrah— Rudra; ekadasa — eleven; vyuhah— whose expansions; tatha— and; asta — eight; tanuh— whose bodies; api — also; asau — he; prayah — usually; pahca-ananah— with five faces; tri-aksah— with three eyes; dasa-bahuh— with ten arms; udiryate — is described.

**Перевод:**

**Regarding Sri Rudra: Rudra has eleven expansions, and he also has eight bodies. He is usually described as having five faces, three eyes, and ten arms.**

**Комментарий:**

As the scriptures relate that the role of Brahma is sometimes assumed by Visnu and sometimes by an empowered jiva, so various scriptures relate that the role of Rudra (Siva) is also assumed in these two ways. Rudra as a direct expansion of Lord Visnu is mentioned in the Srimad-Bhagavatam First Canto, in a verse that describes the Supreme Lord assuming the forms of all three guna-avataras.

The original Rudra expands himself in many forms in the material world, including as the eleven Rudras:

*ajaikapad ahirbradhno*  
*virupakso tha raivatah*  
*haras ca bahurupas ca*  
*tryambakas ca suresvarah*  
*savitras ca jayantas ca*  
*pinaki caparajitah*

**“Lord Siva appears as Ajaikapat, Ahirbradhna, Virupaksa, Raivata, Hara, Bahu-rupa, the best of demigods Tryambaka, Savitra, Jayanta, Pinaki, and Aparajita.” (Mahabharata, Santi-parva 201.18)**

He also expands as eight siva-lihga incarnations (presiding over eight elements), who are worshiped as deities:

*prthivi salilam tejo*  
*vayur akasam eva ca*  
*surya-candramasau soma-*  
*yaji cety asta-murtayah*

**“His eight deity forms preside over earth, water, fire, air, ether, the sun, the moon, and the offerer of Soma sacrifice” (Mahabharata, Santi-parva 201.19)**

Lord Rudra is “usually described as having five faces” because sometimes he is seen with only one, as in that form seen within the layer of water that covers the universe.

### Text 27

*kvacij jiva-visesatvam*  
*harasyoktam vidher iva*  
*tat tu sesa-vad evastam*  
*tad-amsatvena kirtanat*

**Пословный перевод:**

kvacit — some; jiva-visesatvam — being a particular jiva; harasya — of Hara; uktam — is said; vidheh — of Brahma; iva — as; tat — that; tu — but; sesa-vat — like Sesa; eva — indeed; astam— let it be; tat — that; amsatvena — in terms of being a partial expansion; kirtanat — by the description.

**Перевод:**

**Some scriptural statements indicate that Lord Hara is an individual jiva, like Brahma. These are descriptions of partial expansions of Hara, similar to some statements about Ananta Sesa.**

**Комментарий:**

Lord Caitanya taught Sanatana Gosvami that Lord Rudra is neither Visnu nor a finite jiva but is in a special, intermediate category of his own (Sri Caitanya-caritamrta, Madhya 20.308). But Srila Baladeva Vidyabhusana, in his commentary on the previous two verses, uses the word isvara in referring to Rudras original appearance in this world, indicating virtual equality with the Personality of Godhead.

Lord Ananta Sesa, the bedstead of Maha-visnu and a direct expansion of Godhead, can empower a jiva to act in His name so that the jiva can hold the material planets on his serpent hoods. Lord Rudra similarly empowers jiva representatives. These are described in many scriptures, beginning with the Rg Veda (10.125.5-6): yam kamaye tam ugrarii krnomi tam brahmanam tarn rsim tam su-medham. “Whomever I choose for the role, I empower as a fearsome Rudra, a Brahma, a sage, or a wise man.”

The Narayana Upanisad (1) states: atha puruso ha vai narayano ’kamayata prajd srjeya. “Then the Purusa Narayana desired, ‘Let me create progeny.’” The Upanisad continues: narayanad brahma jayate narayanad rudro jdyate narayanat prajapatir jayate narayanad indro jayate narayanad astau vasavo narayanad ekadasa rudra narayanad dvadasadityah. “From Narayana, Brahma was born. From Narayana, Rudra was born. From Narayana, Prajapati was born. From Narayana, Indra was born. From Narayana, the eight Vasus were born. From Narayana, the eleven Rudras were born. From Narayana, the twelve Adityas were born.”

The Maha Upanisad (1-2) states: eko ha vai narayana asin na brahma nesanah. tasya dhyananta-sthasya lalatat try-aksah sula-panih puruso jayata bibhrad chriyam satyam brahma-caryam tapo vairagyam. “There was only Narayana, not Brahma or Siva. While He was absorbed in meditation, there appeared from His forehead a person with three eyes holding a trident in his hand and displaying the opulences of truth, celibacy, austerity, and renunciation.”

The Rudras depicted in these and the following passages are empowered jivas, since they take birth and have other limitations.

*prajapatim ca rudram capy*  
*aham eva srjami vai*  
*tau hi math na vijanito*  
*mama maya-vimohitau*

**“I alone create Prajapati Brahma and Rudra. Both of them, bewildered by My mayay fail to know Me in truth.” (Mahabharata, Moksa-dharma)**

*brahma sambhus tathdivarkas*  
*candramas ca satakratuh*  
*evam-adyas talhaivanye*  
*yukta vaisnava-tejasa*  
*jagat-karyavasdne tu*  
*viyujyante ca tejasa*  
*vitejasas ca te sarve*  
*pancatvam upayanti vai*

**“Brahma, Sambhu (Rudra), the gods of the sun and moon, Indra, and others are empowered with the potency of Lord Visnu. When the period of the manifested material creation ends, their powers are withdrawn; they become powerless, and their forms return to the material elements from which they were born” (Visnu-dharma Purana)**

### Text 28

*harah purusa-dhamatvan*  
*nirgunah praya eva sah*  
*vikaravan iha tamo-*  
*yogat sarvaih pratiyate*  
*yatad sri-dasame,*  
*sivah sakti-yutah sasvat*  
*tri-lingo guna-samvrtah*  
*iti.*

**Пословный перевод:**

harah — Hara; purusa— of the Purusa; dhamatvat— because of being a personal expansion; nirgunah — transcendental to the material modes; pravah — for the most part; eva — indeed; sah — he; vikara-van — subject to transformation; iha — in this world; tamah— with the mode of ignorance; yogat — due to association; sarvaih — by all; pratiyate — is perceived; yatad — as; sri-dasame — in the Tenth Canto; sivah — Lord Siva; sakti— with his energy, material nature; yutah— united; sasvat — always; tri— three; lingah— whose manifest features; guna— by the modes; samvrtah — prayed to; id — thus.

**Перевод:**

**When Lord Hara is a personal expansion of the Purusa, he is nearly transcendental to the material modes. But because of his contact with the mode of ignorance, all in this world perceive him as subject to transformation. We find in the Tenth Canto s10.88.3\] that “Lord Siva is always united with his personal energy, the material nature. He manifests three features in response to the entreaties of nature’s three modes.”**

**Комментарий:**

As mentioned in the First Canto verse that calls the three guna-avataras direct expansions of the Supreme Person, this Lord Hara is transcendental to the modes of nature. His transcendental position differs from that of the limited jivas when they assume the roles of Lord Rudras expansions. Lord Hara is purusa-dhama, nondifferent in substance from Lord Visnu.

As indicated in this verse by the words nirgunah prayah, “nearly transcendental,” Lord Hara sometimes allows himself to be covered by ignorance. It is generally thought that his association with matter subjects him to material change, but in truth he is changeless.

Lord Rudra is eternally related with material nature in her neutral state of equilibrium. When her modes become agitated and develop the visible creation, he becomes tri-linga, surrounded from a distance by the three modes.

Lord Rudra is famous for being covered by the mode of ignorance. How, then, can one correctly call him tri-linga? The answer is that the modes of nature always intermingle, so when Rudra contacts tamo-guna he also contacts sattva and rajas. The Bhagavatam concludes that only ordinary people consider him covered by the modes.

This verse explains how Lord Rudra remains transcendental to the material modes while apparently being affected by contact with the mode of ignorance. The Supreme Lord chooses to take charge of the mode of ignorance and thus expands Himself for that specific purpose without giving up His transcendental nature.
